summary: Template assembly tool pack, stdlib only and deliberately free: it is mechanism, and gating the mechanism that makes an agent's output correct only makes free-tier output worse. tpl-build.py assembles one source template or an ordered block set into Markdown plus a self-contained HTML copy, resolving every declared parameter explicit value, then project store, then declared default, then ask — and a required parameter that reaches the end of that order with nothing to fill it is refused by name rather than substituted empty, which is the difference between a template that fails loudly and a document shipped with a hole in it. The template language is {{name}} substitution plus sections gated on `when: var in [literal, ...]` and nothing else: expressions, loops, filters, Mustache partials, dotted paths, YAML anchors, block scalars and every other construct are each refused by name, because the same assembler runs on behalf of other accounts and a general template language there is a server-side template injection surface. An assembly is blocks plus literal passthrough, because measured over the corpus blocks cover the envelope and the median template shares no bytes with any other: --use takes block references and .md file paths in one ordered list, and a section matching no block is assembled from literals rather than treated as an error. The Markdown to HTML renderer is partial on purpose and says so — headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, fenced code, blockquotes, links, emphasis — escaping everything else, and it runs two escaping paths that never meet: source text is escaped entity-preservingly, so the 58-file family that already stores <artefact_id> is not double-escaped into visible entities, while a substituted value is held as an opaque sentinel through the whole render and escaped unconditionally at the end, so it can neither open a tag nor forge a heading nor break out of a table cell, and only http, https, mailto and relative hrefs are ever resolved. A successful build then remembers what it was given: every --set or --values answer is written to the project store so the next build asks for less, while a value that came from a declared default is deliberately never persisted, because freezing a default means a later change to the block silently stops taking effect and nothing in the project explains why; --no-remember opts out. tpl-params.py is the ask channel: it lists every declared parameter with its type, requiredness, default and whether the project store already answers it, and emits as JSON exactly which parameters are unresolved and the question to ask for each, flagging a text parameter as prose an LLM composes rather than a value a user types. It manages the store at {project}/.faion/template-params.json and a sensitive parameter never reaches it: the store records that the parameter exists and its placeholder, never the value, and any value matching a known secret shape is refused whatever the declaration says. tpl-migrate.py is the third tool and the one that makes the other two reachable for the 1,670 templates carrying <Angle> placeholders and the 556 carrying [bracket] ones: it extracts every candidate placeholder with its position, its heading and the label beside it, proposes a snake_case name, a guessed type and a description drafted from that surrounding context rather than invented, and emits the declaration plus the rewritten body to stdout or a chosen path — the template itself is never touched without --write. What it refuses to do is the point: a placeholder is not automatically a parameter, so prose guidance to a reader, a bare FILL carrying no name, a choice list or date format with no label to name it, a placeholder inside a code fence or code span, an already-HTML-escaped <name> and two placeholders that normalise onto one name are each reported by reason and LEFT ALONE, because a declaration for something that was never a parameter makes tpl-build refuse a build by name forever after. Every rewrite is parsed back before it is written and dropped whole if it does not round-trip, and a template that already declares variables is refused a second block rather than merged. --report runs the same analysis over every template under a root and prints the migration surface — how many map cleanly, how many are prose, which proposed names recur across the corpus and are therefore the parameters worth standardising — which is the table that says whether migration is a week or a quarter. tpl-jinja.py and tpl-render.py are the Jinja form of the same job (.aidocs/conventions/template-jinja-migration.md): tpl-jinja converts one Markdown template into <name>.md.j2, a self-contained <name>.html.j2 generated FROM THE MARKDOWN SOURCE STRUCTURE rather than by converting a rendered document at runtime, and a draft-07 <name>.vars.schema.json that $refs skills/faion/templates/vars-dictionary.schema.json wherever a canonical entry exists and carries a local definition plus an x-faion-todo where it does not. It proposes and never decides: a prose placeholder, a placeholder that repeats down a table's body rows (there are no loops to express it with), a collision and a code-fence placeholder are each reported by reason and left exactly where they are, and a template whose placeholders are already HTML-escaped, one that declares sections:, one carrying a raw Jinja delimiter and one with an undeclared {{x}} are each refused whole rather than guessed at. Nothing is written without --write, and every generated pair is parsed and rendered before the write — including a check that the Markdown renders identically to the pre-Jinja substitution of the same source, so the migration cannot silently change what the corpus emits. tpl-render.py is the consumer: SandboxedEnvironment, autoescape on for HTML and off for Markdown, and StrictUndefined so a missing variable is refused by name instead of rendered as an empty string. It never double-renders — template source comes from a file and values are bound as context, never the other way round, which is the single rule that keeps the injection surface at zero — and it checks values against the schema first, so an unknown key, a wrong type, a value outside an enum, a value for a sensitive variable and anything shaped like a credential are each refused before anything renders. Jinja is this pack's one declared dependency; both tools import it inside a guard and exit 2 with an install line rather than half-working without it.

dependencies.why: tpl-jinja.py and tpl-render.py produce and consume Jinja templates. A hand-rolled substitution engine is what the corpus already had, and reimplementing autoescape, a sandbox and StrictUndefined is a worse trade than one declared dependency.
